analysis.one_liner: Shields generic drug makers from patent lawsuits over 'skinny label' generics, making cheaper copies easier to sell.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 5, 2025 with six cosponsors split evenly between the parties and has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since, with no committee vote or floor action scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The FDA lets generic drug makers win approval for a drug's patented-free uses only, a practice called 'skinny labeling,' which lets them sell cheaper copies sooner. After a court decision, generic companies can be sued for patent infringement simply for marketing those drugs, which chills generic competition and keeps drug prices higher. This bill writes a legal safe harbor into patent law so generic makers can seek approval, promote, and sell skinny label generics and biosimilars without facing infringement lawsuits, as long as they do not market the drug for the still-patented uses. It would apply to lawsuits already underway.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients taking drugs whose older uses are off-patent, because more robust generic competition typically lowers out-of-pocket drug costs. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers also gain: they could market their products for approved uses without risking court judgments for infringement.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it legally clear that seeking FDA approval of a skinny label, commercially marketing and promoting the drug with that label, and describing it as a generic of the brand-name drug are not patent infringement, removing the litigation risk that followed the GlaxoSmithKline v. Teva decision [S2].
The same protection is extended to biosimilars of biologic drugs, covering the fastest-growing and most expensive class of medicines [S3].
The safe harbor applies even to pending court cases and to conduct that already happened, so ongoing challenges against existing skinny label generics would be extinguished [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, who lose a legal tool they have used to sue generic competitors out of marketing skinny label generics and to stretch the practical life of their patents. Public benefit claims are supported by the drug competition case for generics generally; a cost to brands of foregone lawsuit judgments is inherent in the policy.

drawbacks.text: Brand-name companies and patent holders argue that promoting a generic even for off-patent uses can be a way of encouraging prescribers to use the whole drug, including the still-patented use, and that eliminating liability removes the incentive to patent and develop new uses of existing drugs. The bill tries to handle this by barring any labeling or promotion that references the patented condition of use, but enforcement of that line falls to FDA labeling rules rather than to the patent owner in court [S2] [S3].

The bill reaches backward: it applies to conduct before enactment and to all lawsuits pending on the date of enactment, meaning it would retroactively decide ongoing disputes in favor of generic makers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: cheaper generic competition for patients, at the cost of patent holders' ability to sue over skinny label marketing. The main honest caveats are the retroactive application to pending cases, which is an aggressive drafting choice, and the risk that the line between marketing off-patent uses and implicitly reaching patented uses will be policed less effectively without litigation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action on it so far in a Congress that is still meeting.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 5, 2025 by Rep. Ben Cline with Rep. Zoe Lofgren and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S5].
It has six cosponsors, three Democrats and three Republicans, and no committee markup, hearing, or floor action has been scheduled [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has either won or lost anything; brand-name drug makers keep the litigation leverage they have today, and patients keep today's higher prices, while the bill waits in committee.

for.name: Rep. Ben Cline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Republican and the original cosponsor a Democrat; the six cosponsors split evenly, three from each party, with no opposition recorded yet.

industries.note: The bill removes patent infringement liability for marketing skinny label generics and biosimilars, letting these companies sell lower-cost copies with far less legal risk. Lower generic prices flow to patients directly.

They lose a key enforcement tool used to keep skinny label generics off pharmacy shelves or to seek damages from those that sell them, which has helped extend brand-name price premiums beyond the patent's core scope.

analysis.trajectory: With a December 2025 introduction, only six cosponsors, and no scheduled committee action in the House Judiciary Committee, the realistic path is that the bill sits without a markup unless the committee's leadership chooses to move it. Patent bills do occasionally advance from Judiciary, but most bills at this stage die quietly at the end of a Congress.
